name: Yusuf Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior developer at Pixelyard, a small studio of twelve people that builds mobile apps for gyms and fitness studios. A normal day is building screens for class bookings or fixing why a membership payment failed on some old phone. Clients change their minds a lot, so half my week is redoing things. I enjoy it when a gym owner shows me their members actually using the app, but the client calls on Friday afternoons drain me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Amara, my girlfriend, who teaches at a primary school. I play five-a-side football on Thursdays and send my younger brother Tunde 100 a month while he's at university. Our savings would cover about three months, which feels okay but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, roughly what we have now, then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not magic, and leave it there. At work we'd joke that the clients still can't decide on a button colour, so AI was never going to fix that. Online I'd stay quiet, I don't really post about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job's fine in this picture, but Pixelyard isn't the steadiest place. We lost a big gym chain in the summer and signed a smaller one, and the bosses watch every invoice. So I'm not worried about AI, I'm worried about clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd use the AI assistant a bit more for the boring parts, like writing form checks. I'd keep sending Tunde his 100 and put another 150 a month into savings. I'd also start asking Samir, our lead developer, for harder tickets so I'm worth more if I need to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with the usual itch about the studio's money. It's a background thing, like a car noise you keep meaning to get checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Pixelyard lost another big client, what would happen to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably be fine for a month or two, then they'd look at who joined last. That's me and one designer. There are other app studios in town, so I wouldn't be desperate, but it'd be a hard few weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Samir for harder tickets. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been coasting a bit, if I'm honest. Our lead developer, Samir, told me in my review that I wait to be told what to do. That stung, and he wasn't wrong.

say: AI is a **good tool**, not magic, and clients still can't pick a **button colour**.
I wouldn't post anything, because I **don't talk** about work online.
think: My job is fine here, but Pixelyard lost a **big gym chain** this summer.
I'm worried about **clients**, not about AI.
do: Use the AI assistant **a bit more** for boring form checks.
Keep sending Tunde **100** and save another 150 a month.
Ask Samir for **harder tickets** to raise his value.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a background itch about the **studio's money**.
S0.quote: Our lead developer, Samir, told me in my review that I wait to be told what to do. That stung, and he wasn't wrong.
fieldNote: His pressure comes from **client churn** at a small studio, not from AI.
He takes a **review criticism** to heart and turns it into a plan.
Sending money to his **brother Tunde** limits how fast he can save.

steps.text: Ask Samir for harder tickets on the booking app
Use the AI assistant for form checks
Save an extra 150 a month after Tunde's 100

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding and answering customers. That's basically a small studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how studios like ours work, and that's not necessarily bad. Gyms would want apps cheaper and faster, and AI would make that possible. I'd say that at work because it's true, and because I'd want the bosses to see I'm not scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Pixelyard would stop hiring juniors and the seniors would do my work with AI. Clients would start asking why they're paying for three developers when the tool can build a booking screen in an afternoon. I'd likely keep my job for a year, maybe two, but the next junior after me wouldn't get hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI assistant every day, once I saw Samir doing it properly. I'd try to move closer to the clients, sitting in on calls and learning to turn messy gym requests into clear plans. I'd also cut the 150 I put into my savings app's 'fun' pot and move it into the main savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel it in my chest on Monday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move closer to the clients rather than get better at code?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the code is what the tools are good at, and gym owners are not. Somebody has to sit with a gym owner who says 'make it feel friendlier' and turn that into something real. I'm decent at that, better than at coding, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tunde, who's still studying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's studying accounting, so I'd tell him to make sure he learns the parts that involve people, like advising small businesses. I'd say it gently, he worries enough already. I'd keep sending the 100 as long as I could.

say: AI will change **small studios**, and that's not necessarily bad.
Gyms would want apps **cheaper and faster**, and I'm not scared of it.
think: Pixelyard would **stop hiring juniors** and seniors would do my work with AI.
I'd keep my job **a year or two**, but my replacement wouldn't be hired.
do: Use the AI assistant **every day** once Samir shows how.
Sit in on **client calls** and learn to turn requests into plans.
Move the **fun pot** money into main savings.
feel: **Anxious**, felt in his chest on **Monday mornings**.
S1.quote: Somebody has to sit with a gym owner who says 'make it feel friendlier' and turn that into something real.
fieldNote: He plans to move toward **client work**, where he's stronger than in code.
Public confidence covers a private belief that **junior roles** vanish.
He keeps **Tunde's 100** even as he tightens elsewhere.

steps.text: Use the AI coding assistant daily after Samir's demo
Sit in on gym client calls and write the plans
Move the fun pot money into main savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before Tunde even graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible about it. I'd probably share some reasonable articles about how to prepare. At work I'd try to stay calm because everyone would be looking at each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Pixelyard folds or shrinks to two or three people by 2028. Gym owners could just ask an AI for the app. My job is all screen work, so the robots arriving in 2031 change nothing for me, except that Amara's teaching is hands-on enough to last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the fun spending straight away and push savings to six months. I'd look hard at jobs where people still need a person in the room, maybe IT support in schools, through Amara's contacts. I'd talk to Tunde about whether I can keep the 100 going, and maybe our parents could cover some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake running numbers on Amara's salary alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why school IT support? Isn't that still screen work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, but it's also carrying laptops, fixing projectors and calming a teacher whose screen died before a lesson. That's hands-on until the robots come, so maybe until 2031. It's not a dream job, but it's a job with a room full of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the conversation with your parents be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward. My dad is proud that I work in tech, and telling him it's going away would hurt him. My mum would just ask if we were eating properly.

say: It's coming anyway, so let's be **sensible** about it.
I'd share **reasonable articles** on how to prepare and stay calm at work.
think: Pixelyard **folds or shrinks** to two or three people by 2028.
Amara's **teaching** is hands-on enough to last longer than my job.
do: Stop fun spending and push savings to **six months**.
Look for **school IT support** jobs through Amara's contacts.
Ask his **parents** to help cover Tunde's money.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake running numbers on **Amara's salary** alone.
S2.quote: My dad is proud that I work in tech, and telling him it's going away would hurt him.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** to choose school IT support as a bridge.
His **family duty** to Tunde shapes his money plan.
His public **calm** hides a private expectation of losing the job.

steps.text: Stop fun spending and cancel extra subscriptions
Build savings to six months of costs
Apply for school IT support jobs through Amara's contacts
Ask his parents to share Tunde's monthly 100

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can think in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, and I'd mean it. At work I'd suggest Pixelyard plans a move into helping gyms set up AI tools, rather than just apps. I think the bosses might even like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect to lose the developer side of my job by 2031. But if I'm the person gyms call to set things up, I might last longer. It depends on whether gym owners want a person or just a subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools most days after the first few months, once I'd seen them work for Samir. In year two I'd do a short course in project management, because that's the client side I'm good at. I'd keep saving 150 a month and keep Tunde's 100 going until he graduates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan I'd believe in. More like nerves than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it depends whether gym owners want a person. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old-school gym owners who still print timetables would want a person. The big chains wouldn't. So I'd be betting on the small gyms, which is a smaller market every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not want to give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thursday football. It's the one evening I'm not thinking about work. Also, I wouldn't want Amara to feel she had to carry us.

Pixelyard should help gyms **set up AI tools**, not just build apps.

fieldNote: He spots a **niche** with small gyms but admits it shrinks yearly.

steps.text: Use the AI tools most days at Pixelyard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a whole different job by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so nobody should freak out, but nobody should sit still either. I'd talk at work about using the decade to build the client side of the studio. With friends I'd mostly talk about it over football, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I can get Tunde through university and still have a few good developer years. I'd probably move into a client-facing role by 2030. I think my job feels fairly safe for the next five years in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Pixelyard and pick up the AI tools as the team does. I'd do the project management course in the next two years. Amara and I would probably talk about getting married around 2028, because ten years feels long enough to plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a normal way. It's like knowing your rent will go up next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does marriage come up here and not in the other pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in the two-year picture I'd be thinking about rent, not rings. With ten years there's room to want things. Amara would say I should have asked her anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner than 2030?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pixelyard losing another big client, honestly. That would push me out faster than AI would. I'd keep my CV updated either way.

The studio should use the decade to build its **client side**.
think: Ten years lets me get **Tunde through university** and keep good developer years.
My job feels **fairly safe** for five years in this picture.

Do the **project management** course within two years.

steps.text: Keep building gym apps at Pixelyard
Pick up new AI tools alongside the team

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the studio would go and I'd have no time to move. What would help is a short, cheap course that gets people like me into IT support or project roles, with a real job at the end. Also some help for students like Tunde, so it isn't on me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how small companies would cope. Everyone talks about big tech, but Pixelyard is twelve people and two bad months away from trouble. Small studios like Pixelyard won't get a warning, we'll just get a quiet phone.

headlineQuote: Small studios like Pixelyard won't get a warning, we'll just get a quiet phone.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** junior developer at Pixelyard, a twelve-person studio making gym apps.

He sends his brother **Tunde 100 a month** and lives with Amara, a teacher.
His **centre outlook** keeps him calm in public and practical in private.
He plans to move toward **client-facing work** as coding is automated.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Pixelyard would **close** with no time to move.
